title: The anatomy of a shadow — Image Wiki
text:
The anatomy of a shadow
  The named parts of light and shade on a solid object — highlight, halftone, core shadow, reflected light, cast shadow, contact shadow — and the rules each one obeys.

  
    Termlight and shadow zones
    Also calledshading zones, form shadow and cast shadow, terminator, core shadow
    Not the same asform shadow vs cast shadow, core shadow vs cast shadow, specular vs diffuse highlight
    Read9 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The partsTwo distinctions to get exactly rightWhy the contact point is the darkest placeWhy reflected light cannot beat the lit sideCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Put an egg on a white table next to a window and look at it ten seconds longer than feels necessary. There is far more there than "light side, dark side": seven things, seven names, seven different rules.
Telling them apart is the most useful skill for spotting an assembled or generated image, because a picture can get the big shapes right and still make these relationships physically impossible. Where the pattern sits on the object is set by Light direction; how sharp its edges are, by Hard and soft light.
The parts

highlighthalftonecore shadowreflected lightcontact shadowcast shadowSix zones, one ball, one lampmatte white ball on a matte floor, small source upper left

Trace it from the top left down and across. The highlight sits where the surface faces the lamp squarely. The halftone is the long, almost-even stretch where the surface has begun to turn away. Then the core shadow arrives as a fast dark band, where the surface has swung past the light completely — a band and not a line, because immediately beyond it the ball starts picking up bounce again.
Now check the two relationships a faked image usually gets wrong. The reflected light on the far rim is lighter than the core band beside it, but it stays clearly darker than any part of the lit side. And the contact shadow where the ball meets the floor is darker than the cast shadow it sits inside — the ball and the floor between them wall off almost the whole sky from that seam, while the open shadow on the floor is still lit by the rest of the room.


The rules that are not obvious from the drawing:
Specular highlight. A reflection of the light source — shaped and coloured like the lamp, not the egg, and sitting wherever the geometry between lamp, surface and eye puts it rather than in the middle of the lit side. Strobist: you can tell a can of Coke is cold without touching it, because condensation turns the highlight's edges soft and matte (Diffuse and specular).
Diffuse highlight, or full light. Where the object's real colour shows. On a black object the full light is still black, which is why dark glossy things have to be described by their speculars instead.
Halftone. Brightness follows the tilt, on a deceptive curve: 30° off, a surface still looks about 94% as bright; at 60°, 73%; at 80°, 45%; then it collapses. Almost all the change is in the last stretch.
Reflected light. Light that hit something else first — table, wall, sky — and came back into the shadow side. It can get strong: James Gurney's ochre building in Toledo, drenched in bounce off an orange building opposite, is more saturated on its shadow side than in direct sun.



Francisco de Zurbarán, Still Life with Lemons, Oranges and a Rose, 1633 (Norton Simon Museum, Pasadena). Public domain.
Every zone in the list, on real objects, under one source. The light comes from the upper left: all three cast shadows — of the plate of lemons, of the basket, of the cup — run to the right, and each object's lit face is its upper left.
Take the lemon on the left of the pewter plate. Its highlight is a soft pale patch on the upper left of the skin, broad rather than a dot, because a lemon is matte. The halftone covers most of the rest of the peel, changing so gradually you cannot say where it begins. The core shadow is the darkest part of the fruit itself, along its lower right — and it stops short of the silhouette, because a thin strip of reflected light off the plate lifts the bottom of the lemon back out of the dark. Compare that strip against the lit top of the same lemon: unmistakably darker. That is the rule that keeps the fruit reading as solid.
Then the two shadows on the table. The cast shadow to the right of the plate is a soft, open grey — blocked from the window but still lit by the rest of the room. The contact shadow under the rim of the plate is a near-black hairline, because nothing gets into that seam at all. Cover the fruit and the plate still reads as sitting on the wood, from that line alone.


Two distinctions to get exactly right
Form shadow versus cast shadow. A form shadow is the object turning away from the light; a cast shadow is the object blocking light from reaching something else. Drawabox: form shading happens on the object, cast shadows are projected onto another surface.
They behave differently, and that is the point. A form shadow's edge is set by the object's curvature and the source size, so it is generally a gradual roll. A cast shadow's edge softens the further it travels from the contact point (Hard and soft light) — so one that is uniformly blurry, or uniformly sharp along its whole length, is suspicious.
Core shadow versus cast shadow. Both dark, both on the shadow side, on different surfaces: the core shadow follows the egg's curvature, the cast shadow is the egg's outline projected onto the table. Merging them is why untrained drawings smear a dark outline around the base of every form.
Why the contact point is the darkest place
A cast shadow's interior is blocked from the window but wide open to the rest of the room — ceiling, far wall, half the sky — so it is dark, not black. The hairline gap where the egg touches the table is blocked from nearly everything, because egg and tabletop wall off almost the whole hemisphere above it. Renderers call this ambient occlusion; Drawabox puts it from the drawing end — turn the light up and shadows burn away until only the deepest cracks survive.
So black lives in crevices, seams, the underside of a collar, the join where a chair leg meets the floor. Not in the middle of a shadow.

no seam hereshadow sits apartFloatingone soft blob, offset, base sitting on clean floorhard dark seamsoftens with distancePlantedshadow anchored on the footprint, near-black at the join

Same box, same lamp, same two rays grazing its top corners. On the left the shadow is a single uniformly soft blob sitting a few centimetres clear of the base, and the bottom edge of the box meets untouched floor — so the box hovers, and the rays land somewhere no shadow is.
On the right the shadow begins on the footprint and never leaves it: near-black in the seam, then softening as it travels away from the contact. Cover everything except the bottom edge of each box and the difference is still obvious. That few-pixel band is what a pasted-in or generated object most often lacks entirely.


This is the highest-value check in the article. An object pasted into a scene, or generated without real light transport, very often has a plausible cast shadow and no seam.
Why reflected light cannot beat the lit side
Reflected light is second-hand twice over: the bouncing surface caught only a fraction of the source, then returns only what it does not absorb — well under half for anything short of a mirror. A fraction of a fraction.
The working rule: on one object under one source, reflected light inside the shadow stays darker than the darkest part of the lit side. Break it and the object reads as a cut-out with a glow behind it. If something in the shadow really is that bright, it is a second source, and it should be casting shadows of its own somewhere.



Juan Sánchez Cotán, Quince, Cabbage, Melon and Cucumber, c. 1602 (San Diego Museum of Art). Public domain.
The same painting runs the experiment twice, and the difference is whether there is anything nearby to catch light or throw it back. One small hard source enters from the upper left: the cut wedge and the cucumber each lay a crisp-edged shadow to the right along the stone ledge, and each has a dark seam where it touches.
On the ledge, the objects get the full sequence — cast shadow, contact seam, and a shadow side kept well above black by the pale stone underneath. Hanging in the void, the quince and the cabbage get none of it: no floor, no wall, nothing behind them, so their shaded sides fall away toward the black of the ground and neither casts a shadow anywhere in the picture. Same painter, same light, same day. Both cast shadows and reflected light need a second surface to exist at all.


Common mistakes

"The darkest part of the picture is the middle of a shadow." It is a contact point; a cast shadow's interior still sees most of the sky. For Value structure that means true black is usually a seam a few pixels wide.
"A shadow that fades out must be soft." It might be running from a close lamp. Fading with distance is Light falloff; fading at the edge is softness.
"The core shadow is the object's shadow." Core shadow on the object, cast shadow on whatever it stands on. Both usually exist and touch.
"Reflected light brightens the shadow side." Slightly. Never past the lit side.
"A highlight is the light part of the object." Two things, one word: the diffuse highlight shows the object's colour, the specular shows the lamp.
"Shadows are grey." A shadow is lit by whatever still reaches it, usually a different colour from the key. See The colour of the light.


Five seconds on any solid object

Where the object meets the ground: a distinct dark seam? No seam means it is floating.
Trace the cast shadow. Does it run away from the light and sharpen as it nears the contact point?
Find the core shadow band on the object. Is there a lighter strip below it from bounce?
Is anything on the shadow side brighter than the lit side? Not physically available under one light.
Does every object agree on one light direction, one shadow softness, one contact darkness?



  
    
      Read next
      
        
          
            
              Hard and soft light
              Whether shadows have crisp edges or fade gradually. It is decided by one thing — how big the light looks from where the subject is standing.
            
          
        
          
            
              Light direction
              Where the light sits relative to the subject and to the camera. It decides where the shadows land and how much of the shaded side you get to see, which is what makes a flat picture look solid.
            
          
        
          
            
              Diffuse and specular
              Light hitting a surface either goes in and comes back out coloured, or bounces straight off keeping the light's own colour. Almost everything a material looks like follows from the split between those two.
            
          
        
          
            
              Naming what is wrong
              A checklist for turning "something looks off" into a specific, defensible sentence about the image.
